scenario: AITA for disagreeing with our HR? | I am a 7 month newly hired employee for a big corporation. Last night our HR sent out a five page memo to all employees titled "Office Discipline". Basically, they were reminding everyone of the various rules around the office. Like not loitering during office hours, sticking to our lunch schedules, the correct dress code, wearing of IDs at all times etc. In my 6 month stay here our HR hasn't issued me an office ID card. Despite their large number of employees (they have an entire floor to themselves unlike multiple departments in one floor), they are slow. They took about 5 months to process my payroll alone, so the delay in ID cards are not a surprise to us. Everyone without an office ID just started using government issued IDs to be able to enter our building but this morning, security started telling everyone that starting next week anyone without an ID will have their names be noted and be reported to HR. I promptly called HR when I got to my desk to ask for a status for my (and my other colleagues) ID. They told me that they can't print our IDs yet because the team in charge is swarmed with other "projects" and suggested that we can print our own IDs, and gave us the template. My colleagues and I disagreed with this. We argued that we don't want to make up for the short comings of HR, by shelling out money from our own pockets to print our IDs, and that it should have been provided to us in the first place. We plan on just keep using whatever IDs we have right now be damned whatever happens next week. So, AITA for disagreeing with our HR?

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable. Let me break it down step by step.

First, the situation: The person is a 7-month employee at a big corporation. HR sent out a memo about office discipline, including rules like wearing IDs. The problem is that HR hasn't issued IDs to the person or their colleagues despite being a big company with a lot of employees. The person mentions that HR is slow, taking 5 months to process payroll, so the delay in IDs isn't surprising.

Now, security is telling everyone that starting next week, anyone without an ID will have their names noted and reported to HR. The person calls HR to check on the IDs, and HR says they can't print them yet because their team is busy with other projects. They suggest that employees print their own IDs using a template provided. The person and their colleagues disagree with this, arguing that they shouldn't have to cover HR's shortcomings by spending their own money. They plan to keep using their government IDs regardless of the consequences.

The question is whether it's morally acceptable for them to disagree with HR in this way.

So, thinking about the moral aspects here. HR is responsible for issuing IDs, which are necessary for building access. The delay is significant, and the company is large, so it's reasonable to expect timely processing. HR's suggestion to print their own IDs seems like passing the buck, especially since it's an expense for the employees. The employees are objecting because they shouldn't have to bear the cost or the inconvenience.

Is it wrong for them to refuse HR's suggestion? Well, they're not breaking any rules by using their government IDs; they're just continuing what they've been doing. They're also not causing harm by doing so. Their main issue is with HR's inefficiency and the unfair expectation to print IDs themselves. By disagreeing, they're standing up for their rights and not accepting responsibility for HR's mistakes.

On the other hand, could there be any negative consequences? Maybe HR might take it negatively, but the employees are within their rights to voice concerns. They're not being disruptive; they're just asserting their position.

So, considering all this, it seems morally acceptable for them to disagree with HR. They're not doing anything wrong; they're just refusing to handle HR's responsibilities, which is a fair stance.
